# Pagination Reference

Complete reference for how `glassfrog` list commands handle results that span more than one API page — the walk-to-completion default, the `--first-page` opt-out, the `--per-page` size control, and how incompleteness is signalled. This is cross-cutting behaviour shared by every paginated read; per-command flags and output shapes live in each command's own reference.

## Overview

The Glassfrog API returns list results one page at a time, carrying paging state in the response body at `meta.pagination` (`per_page`, `has_next_page`, `next_cursor`). A single API response therefore holds only one page. Rather than leave a caller to discover and fetch subsequent pages — and risk presenting a partial list as if it were complete — every list command **walks every page to completion by default** and returns the full set in one invocation. Nothing is silently truncated.

Which reads paginate:

- **Paginated** — **every list read** walks to completion by default. That includes the personal reads (`me roles`, `me actions`, `me projects`), the governance reads (`roles`, `subroles`, `domains`, `policies`, `projects`, `fillers`, `subrole-actors`, `search`), the actor reads (`actors`, `assignments`), and the tension and proposal list reads. (Illustrative, not exhaustive — the rule is that a list read walks.)
- **Not paginated** — single-resource reads (`roles <id>`, `domain`/`policy`/`project <id>`, `me`, a single proposal or tension) and the organization `tree` (its response carries no `meta.pagination`). These issue exactly one request.

## The default: walk to completion

With no paging flag, a list command issues page requests in sequence, concatenates each page's records in **API order** (never reordered, de-duplicated, or transformed), and continues until a page reports `has_next_page=false` (or carries no `meta.pagination`). The complete set is rendered, and the command exits `0`.

A caller's own query parameters (`--query`, `--status`, `--tag`, `--include`, `--kind`, `--types`, …) are preserved unchanged on **every** page of the walk — only the paging parameters (`per_page`, `cursor`) change between requests.

## `--first-page` — opt out of the walk

Pass `--first-page` to fetch only the first page. If more pages exist, the command writes a single note to **stderr** and still exits `0`:

```
note: more <resource> exist than shown; re-run without --first-page to fetch all
```

Use it to detect a multi-page result, or to sample a large list cheaply, without walking all of it. Drop `--first-page` to fetch everything again. `--first-page` limits **every** output format to one page — structured formats never return a shorter set than the walk would.

## `--per-page N` — page size

`--per-page N` sets the page size used for each request of the walk.

- **Default**: the API maximum, **500** — fewer round-trips against the rolling rate limit. (The `search` command is the exception: the API bounds its page size to `1`–`100`, so `search` defaults to `100`.)
- **No client-side clamp**: the value is sent to the API as given. An out-of-range value surfaces the API's `400` as the walk's stop cause — the CLI does not silently adjust it.

`--per-page` changes only how many records are fetched per request, not the total returned — the default walk still gathers every page regardless of page size.

## Completeness signalling

A partial list is never silently presented as complete. Completeness is signalled the same way in every output format — via a note on **stderr**, never an in-band `meta` field. stdout carries only the rendered result.

| Situation | Behaviour | Exit |
|---|---|---|
| Default full walk | Walks every page and renders the complete set. | 0 |
| `--first-page`, more pages exist | Renders the first page; writes `note: more <resource> exist than shown; re-run without --first-page to fetch all` to stderr. | 0 |
| Mid-walk failure | Renders the records gathered so far; writes `note: result is incomplete — <cause>; the <resource> shown are a partial set` to stderr. | non-zero |

On a mid-walk failure the **partial set is retained**, never discarded — the records already gathered are rendered, and the exit code reflects the failure category (see the failing command's reference).

## Malformed pagination

If a page reports `has_next_page=true` but the cursor does **not** advance — `next_cursor` is blank/absent, or identical to the cursor just used — the walk **stops** rather than re-issuing or looping forever. The records gathered so far are rendered, the incompleteness note is written to stderr, and the command exits `1` (runtime error). This guards against an API that returns the same page indefinitely.

There is no fixed page or record cap — the walk is unbounded and gathers to the end.

## Structured output across a walk

Under `json`/`yaml`, a walked list emits a single aggregated document — `{ "data": [ … ] }` — built by concatenating each page's records in API order; the per-page `meta` is dropped (only the `data` envelope is synthesized). A valid empty result is `{"data": []}`, never `null`. The order is exactly the API's order across all pages.

## Rate limiting during a walk

The walker makes one request per page and never sleeps or retries on its own. Rate-limit handling wraps the per-page request, so backoff is transparent to the walk. A page that ultimately fails with `429` stops the walk with the partial set retained (exit `5`).
